title: Bamberg Witch Trials Begin: Largest German Prosecution
description:
The Bamberg witch trials, conducted between 1623 and 1631 in the Prince-Bishopric of Bamberg in Franconia, were among the largest witch persecutions in European history, resulting in over 300 executions including some of the most prominent members of Bamberg's civic elite. The persecution began under Prince-Bishop Johann Georg II Fuchs von Dornheim, known as the Hexenbischof (witch bishop), and was driven by a combination of religious zealotry, fiscal pressure (confiscated property financed the persecution), and the chain-accusation dynamics that characterize large-scale prosecutions. Among the executed were several prominent officials including Vice Chancellor Dr. Georg Haan, four burgomasters, and the Chancellor of the Prince-Bishop, Johannes Junius.

The Bamberg trials are historically significant not only for their scale but for the remarkable documentary record they left. Johannes Junius, executed in 1628, wrote a farewell letter to his daughter from his cell that survives and provides one of the most moving first-person accounts of a witch trial from the accused's perspective. Junius described how, unable to endure the torture, he had eventually confessed to things he insisted were entirely false, naming his wife and others to satisfy his torturers. The letter illuminates the systematic way in which torture produced confessions and chain-accusations, as each accused person named others under duress.

The trials were eventually halted by Imperial intervention — the Reichshofrat issued a mandate in 1630-1631 critical of the proceedings — and by the broader disruption caused by the Thirty Years' War. Friedrich Spee's Cautio Criminalis (1631), though not referring to Bamberg by name, was written in direct response to what Spee had witnessed as confessor to Würzburg victims and described the torture and procedural abuses evident across the Franconian trials. The Bamberg persecution remains one of the most thoroughly documented examples of a self-feeding judicial massacre.
historiographical_note: H.C. Erik Midelfort's Witch Hunting in Southwestern Germany 1562-1684 (1972) established the pattern-based analysis of German mass prosecutions that placed Bamberg and Würzburg within a comparative framework. Lyndal Roper's Witch Craze (2004) provides extended analysis of the German prosecutions with attention to gender, body, and fantasy. The Junius letter has been edited and translated multiple times and analyzed as evidence of how torture operated to produce self-reinforcing confession chains. Brian Levack's statistics treat the Bamberg-Würzburg cluster as representing the worst excess of the German 'witch craze.'
source_method: Bamberg witch trial records (partially preserved in archives); Johannes Junius letter; Midelfort (1972); Roper (2004)
